Observation: A thick, gel-like slurry forms during reagent addition (e.g., when the acid-chloride mixture is charged to the substrate solution), making stirring difficult and causing "clumping" of solids.
Hypothesis: change_of_addition_order_or_feed_profile, solvent_change_for_solubility, improved_mixing_or_impeller_design - changing the feed sequence, selecting a solvent that keeps the reaction mixture fluid, and/or upgrading the agitation hardware will keep the slurry homogenous and improve conversion.
Experiment: A DoE was run varying (i) the addition direction (substrate into acid vs. acid into substrate), (ii) the reactor temperature (-10 °C -> 0 °C) and (iii) the impeller type (standard vs. high-shear). The optimal condition was inverse addition of the substrate into a pre-cooled acid stream with a high-shear impeller, which eliminated clumps and gave >95 % conversion.
additional_details: The symptom becomes more pronounced above ~10 kg scale where heat removal is slower; the same strategy works in both batch and continuous-flow impinging-jet reactors. Monitoring slurry viscosity in-line (e.g., torque on the motor) can be used as an early warning.

Observation: During reagent addition the reactor temperature rises abruptly (10-15 °C above set-point) and sometimes exceeds the temperature limit for the protecting group or acid-labile functionality.
Hypothesis: temperature_setpoint_or_temperature_ramp_optimization, improved_heat_transfer_or_temperature_control_hardware, pressure_or_gas_headspace_optimization - tighter temperature control, pre-cooling feeds, and better heat-exchange hardware will damp the spike.
Experiment: A series of temperature-ramp studies were performed in a jacketed reactor: (i) pre-cool the acid stream to -10 °C, (ii) add the substrate over 30 min with a controlled ramp, (iii) install a high-efficiency coil heat-exchanger. The temperature excursion was limited to <2 °C and the epimerisation impurity dropped from 0.3 % to <0.05 %.
additional_details: The symptom is especially acute for reactions that generate gases (CO₂, H₂) or involve strong acids (HBr, HCl). Real-time temperature monitoring with a PID controller is recommended for scale-up.

Symptom: Clogging / fouling of reactors or mixers
Observation: Solid material builds up in feed lines, static mixers, or Y-junctions, leading to pressure spikes, pump stall, or complete blockage (e.g., "gel/foam" trapped in a Y-mixer).
Hypothesis: clogging_or_fouling_mitigation, custom_or_novel_reactor_design, improved_mixing_or_impeller_design - redesign the hardware (larger-diameter mixers, smoother surfaces) and/or introduce periodic solvent rinses to keep the flow path clear.
Experiment: A custom 3-D-printed Y-mixer with enlarged outlet diameter (0.25 in) and Hastelloy construction was fabricated. The process was run with a high-velocity THF rinse (10 L min⁻¹) after each batch. Clogging events dropped from 4 per 10 batches to 0, and overall isolated yield increased from 71 % to 61 % crude assay.
additional_details: Periodic "flush" steps are essential for any continuous-flow operation that generates solids. Monitoring pressure drop across the mixer provides an early indicator of fouling.

Observation: Assay yields plateau at 60-80 % despite stoichiometric reagent excess; residual starting acid or intermediate is detected by HPLC.
Hypothesis: optimization_of_reagent_stoichiometry, optimization_of_acid_or_base_stoichiometry, solvent_change_for_solubility - fine-tune the equivalents of acid (e.g., HBr, SOCl₂) and control water content to drive the equilibrium to completion.
Experiment: A response-surface DoE varied HBr equivalents (4-8 eq) and water content (0-5 vol %). The optimum (8 eq HBr, 2 vol % water) gave >98 % conversion with no detectable intermediate. The same stoichiometry was transferred to a 100 kg batch with consistent results.
additional_details: The symptom often appears together with viscous slurry formation; increasing reagent load can also raise exotherm risk, so temperature control must be revisited concurrently.

Observation: During acid addition a two-phase mixture forms (e.g., aqueous acid over organic solvent) that creates emulsions, uneven feeding, or "turbid" streams that are hard to pump.
Hypothesis: solvent_change_for_solubility, solvent_system_optimization_or_cosolvent_addition, change_of_additive - adjust solvent polarity, add co-solvents to improve miscibility, or use antisolvents that promote rapid phase separation.
Experiment: A solvent-screening matrix compared pure toluene, toluene + 10 % MeOH, and pure MeOH as reaction media for the thionyl-chloride step. The toluene + 10 % MeOH system eliminated the emulsion, allowed smooth pumping, and maintained >90 % conversion. Inline phase-separator tests confirmed rapid disengagement.
additional_details: The symptom is often linked to the "mixability" category; a simple viscosity measurement or visual inspection of the feed stream can flag it early. Adding a small amount of a polar co-solvent (e.g., MeOH) is a low-cost mitigation.

Observation:
Isolated yield falls markedly (>= 10 % loss) when the reaction is run beyond
~ 0.1 mol or on kilogram-scale batches.
Hypothesis:
optimization_of_reagent_stoichiometry, optimization_of_catalyst_loading,
change_of_oxidant_or_oxidation_protocol, temperature_setpoint_or_temperature_ramp_optimization,
solvent_change_for_solubility - increasing oxidant/catalyst equivalents,
adjusting temperature ramps, or switching to a solvent that improves
mass-transfer should restore conversion and prevent side-products.
Experiment:
A DoE screening was performed varying (i) oxidant equivalents (1.0-2.5 eq),
(ii) catalyst loading (5-20 mol %), (iii) temperature profile (-10 °C -> rt
vs. isothermal 25 °C), and (iv) solvent (DCM vs. toluene). The optimal
condition (2.5 eq oxidant, 15 mol % catalyst, controlled-ramp) gave >= 95 %
isolated yield on 150 g scale.
additional_details:
The symptom is more pronounced for substrates with limited solubility; a
solvent-change to a more polar chlorinated medium (e.g., DCM) often
supplements stoichiometric adjustments. Monitoring conversion by inline GC
during scale-up helps catch the drop early.

Observation:
Rapid temperature rise (>= 10 °C within minutes) or uncontrolled hot spots
during oxidation, often accompanied by pressure increase.
Hypothesis:
temperature_setpoint_or_temperature_ramp_optimization,
improved_heat_transfer_or_temperature_control_hardware,
thermal_runaway_mitigation_or_quench_safety_modification,
pressure_or_gas_headspace_optimization - applying controlled feeds,
enhanced jacket cooling, DSC-guided safety limits, or vented head-space
prevents temperature spikes.
Experiment:
A calorimetric study (DSC) defined the maximum adiabatic temperature rise.
The batch reactor was equipped with a double-jacket heat exchanger and a
semi-batch H₂O₂ feed (0.5 mL min⁻¹) controlled by a PID loop. Temperature
was held <= 30 °C throughout a 200 g run, eliminating runaway.
additional_details:
For gas-phase oxidants (O₂, air) maintaining O₂ mole fraction below the
limiting-oxygen-concentration (LOC) by diluting with N₂ also curtails
exothermicity. Real-time temperature probes at multiple locations are
essential for early detection.

Observation:
Formation of distinct organic/aqueous layers, gas bubbles, or slurries that
persist despite agitation; conversion drops or becomes erratic.
Hypothesis:
phase_behavior_or_biphasic_system_optimization,
solvent_change_for_solubility,
change_of_additive,
change_of_catalyst_or_ligand_identity,
improved_mixing_or_impeller_design - redesigning the reactor geometry,
adding co-solvents, using solid-supported TEMPO, or switching to a
single-phase solvent system improves interfacial contact and conversion.
Experiment:
A pilot-scale flow reactor was fitted with a T-shaped static mixer and
peristaltic pumps (instead of syringe pumps). The biphasic DCM/H₂O system
was replaced by a homogeneous NMP/TEMPO system (solid-supported catalyst).
Conversion rose from 55 % to > 95 % with stable pressure and no bubble-induced
fluctuations.
additional_details:
Gas-liquid separators downstream of the reactor (e.g., Microsaic MiDas)
can dampen bubble-induced MS signal noise, as shown for Ru-catalysed flow
oxidations. Monitoring phase ratios by inline NIR helps maintain the optimum
mixing regime.

Observation:
Product yield or selectivity declines after several hours or multiple
batch cycles, despite constant feed composition.
Hypothesis:
change_of_catalyst_or_ligand_identity,
optimization_of_catalyst_loading,
temperature_setpoint_or_temperature_ramp_optimization,
pressure_or_gas_headspace_optimization - switching to a more robust
catalyst support, increasing catalyst loading, modestly raising temperature
to re-activate the catalyst, or controlling gas composition to limit NOₓ
formation can restore activity.
Experiment:
For the CuI/TEMPO system, the support was changed from γ-Al₂O₃ to mesoporous
alumina, and the O₂ feed was reduced to 5 % in N₂. After a 150 h run, the
aldehyde yield remained > 90 % without the earlier decline observed with the
original catalyst.
additional_details:
Periodic regeneration (e.g., brief oxidative wash) can extend catalyst life.
Online UV-vis monitoring of metal leaching provides early warning of deactivation.

Observation:
Work-up requires multiple extractions, chromatography, or special quench
steps to eliminate metal residues, by-products, or inorganic salts; yields
are lost in the purification stage.
Hypothesis:
improved_impurity_purge_or_byproduct_control,
improved_quench_or_neutralization,
drying_or_isolation_process_optimization,
crystallization_solvent_or_antisolvent_optimization,
improved_in_process_control_or_analytical_method - introducing chelating
quench (EDTA), phase-selective extractions, or crystallisation from a
co-solvent can purge impurities efficiently and improve overall recovery.
Experiment:
In the Cu/TEMPO oxidation, an aqueous EDTA wash (0.1 M) was added post-reaction,
followed by a single liquid-liquid extraction with EtOAc. Copper levels fell
below 1 ppm and isolated aldehyde yield increased from 78 % to 92 % without
chromatography.
additional_details:
For reactions forming volatile aldehydes (e.g., 447), telescoping the crude
product directly into the next step avoids isolation altogether. Inline
MS monitoring with external reference standards prevents impurity buildup.

Observation: A solid or waxy precipitate appears during the reaction, giving a visibly heterogeneous mixture (e.g., waxy solids, lumps of solid reductant, slurry that does not fully dissolve).
Hypothesis: improved_mixing_or_impeller_design, change_of_addition_order_or_feed_profile, solvent_change_for_solubility - improving agitation, feeding the solid as a solution, or switching to a solvent that keeps all components in solution should restore homogeneity and give reproducible conversion.
Experiment: A DoE screening of agitation speed (250 -> 600 rpm), addition mode (single-charge solid vs. split-charge solution), and solvent (2-propanol, MeCN, EtOAc) was performed on a 10 g pilot reactor. The optimal condition combined a 600 rpm impeller, three equal portions of a 1 M NaBH(OAc)₃ solution in EtOAc, and a co-solvent (MeCN) that kept the amine fully dissolved. Conversion rose from 45 % to > 95 % with no visible solids.
additional_details: The symptom is often first noticed as a "waxy" layer on the reactor wall (Pd/C case) or as "lumpy" reductant after addition. The remedy may require hardware changes (larger impeller) for very large reactors; the same principle applies to both batch and flow.

Symptom: Hydrogen / gas evolution on solid addition
Observation: Rapid evolution of gas (H₂ or HCN) is observed when a solid reductant (e.g., NaBH₄, NaCNBH₃, Na(OAc)₃BH) is added to a protic solvent, sometimes forming bubbles or pressure spikes.
Hypothesis: change_of_reductant_or_reduction_protocol, thermal_runaway_mitigation_or_quench_safety_modification - switching to a soluble reductant solution or a less gas-producing reagent, and adding temperature/pressure interlocks, eliminates the gas burst and stabilises the reduction step.
Experiment: A comparative run replaced solid NaBH₄ with a 1 M NaBH₄ solution in DMSO and introduced a controlled addition pump. Simultaneously, a temperature probe with a 30 °C interlock was installed. On a 5 kg scale the gas evolution was reduced to background levels, pressure stayed below 1 bar gauge, and isolated yield improved from 48 % to 71 %.
additional_details: For cyanoborohydride routes, the HCN risk is mitigated by isolating the imine first and then reducing with NaBH₄ (non-HCN-generating). The same principle applies to any solid hydride that reacts with protic media.

Observation: During reagent addition (often NaBH(OAc)₃ or NaBH₄) the reactor temperature rises abruptly (10-30 °C above setpoint) within minutes, sometimes exceeding the recommended limit.
Hypothesis: temperature_setpoint_or_temperature_ramp_optimization, thermal_runaway_mitigation_or_quench_safety_modification, improved_heat_transfer_or_temperature_control_hardware - lower the addition temperature, add the reagent dropwise, and equip the reactor with efficient cooling jackets or external heat exchangers to keep the temperature within a safe window.
Experiment: A temperature-ramp study added NaBH(OAc)₃ over 50 min while maintaining the reactor at 17 °C (instead of 25 °C). A stainless-steel jacket with a 5 °C coolant inlet was installed. The maximum temperature rise was limited to 5 °C, and the isolated yield increased from 48 % to 69 % with no impurity formation.
additional_details: The symptom is often first detected by a temperature probe alarm. For flow reactors, the same principle is achieved by diluting the reductant stream and using a high-surface-area heat-exchange coil.

Observation: Reactions require > 12 h (often 24 h) to reach acceptable conversion, and even then a noticeable amount of starting material remains (10-30 %).
Hypothesis: temperature_setpoint_or_temperature_ramp_optimization, change_of_reductant_or_reduction_protocol, batch_to_flow_or_flow_process_implementation - raising the temperature (within stability limits), using a more reactive reductant (e.g., 2-picoline.BH₃), or moving to a continuous flow platform shortens the residence time while maintaining selectivity.
Experiment: A side-by-side comparison was performed: (A) Na(OAc)₃BH at 5 °C for 24 h (baseline) vs. (B) 2-picoline.BH₃ at 50 °C for 1 h. The flow version of (B) used a three-stage plug-flow reactor with 1 min residence per stage. Conversion rose from 70 % to > 99 % and overall throughput increased 12-fold.
additional_details: When temperature cannot be increased due to impurity sensitivity, a two-stage addition of reductant (portion-wise) can maintain reducing power over the extended period, as demonstrated for the 20 h "long-reaction" case.

Observation: Assay yields or impurity profiles fluctuate between runs (e.g., 80 % vs 90 % conversion, or variable over-alkylation) even when nominally identical procedures are followed.
Hypothesis: change_of_addition_order_or_feed_profile, optimization_of_reagent_stoichiometry, improved_in_process_control_or_analytical_method - standardising semi-batch feeding, tightening stoichiometric windows, and implementing real-time PAT (e.g., inline NMR or viscosity probes) reduce the sources of variability.
Experiment: A controlled semi-batch feeding protocol (10 % of amine added every 5 min) was programmed on a 5 L reactor, and an inline UV-vis probe monitored imine concentration. Stoichiometry was tightened to 1.3 equiv amine. Yield reproducibility improved from a 15 % spread to < 2 % spread over ten consecutive runs.
additional_details: Variability can also be linked to raw-material impurity levels; a supplier-variability management program (e.g., tighter acceptance criteria) further stabilises the process.

Observation: Sudden rise of +10 °C or more in the reactor temperature during hydrogenation (hot-spot formation).
Hypothesis: temperature_setpoint_or_temperature_ramp_optimization, improved_heat_transfer_or_temperature_control_hardware - by controlling the temperature ramp, adding external cooling or upgrading the jacket, the exotherm can be dissipated safely.
Experiment: A DoE on temperature-ramp rate and external coolant flow was performed in a 5 L autoclave; the optimal ramp (2 °C min⁻¹) and a downstream heat-exchanger kept the temperature <= 30 °C above set-point, eliminating hot-spots and preserving product purity.
additional_details: The symptom becomes more pronounced when H₂ pressure or substrate concentration is increased; it is also observed with substrates that undergo rapid hydrogen uptake (e.g., α-β-unsaturated aldehydes, pinene). Monitoring with an inline thermocouple is essential.

Observation: Low conversion or long reaction times despite sufficient catalyst and H₂ pressure; slurry becomes highly viscous or gas-liquid interfacial area appears limited (e.g., "plateaued conversion", "viscous slurry").
Hypothesis: improved_mixing_or_impeller_design, custom_or_novel_reactor_design, phase_behavior_or_biphasic_system_optimization - by installing high-speed impellers, oscillatory baffled reactors or redesigning the vessel to improve gas holdup, the mass-transfer limitation is removed.
Experiment: Scale-up from 0.5 L to 10 L was tested with a conventional stirrer (ineffective) and then with an OBR (oscillatory baffled reactor). The OBR increased k_La by ~ 3-fold, reducing reaction time from 12 h to 45 min and giving consistent conversion.
additional_details: The issue is especially acute for neat (solvent-free) substrates (pinene, β-pinene) or highly fluorinated solvents (HFIP). Adding a small co-solvent or increasing gas pressure can also alleviate the limitation, but mechanical mixing improvements are usually more robust.

Observation: Drop in conversion after several batches or cycles, need to increase catalyst loading, or observation of coke/metal leaching on the catalyst after reaction.
Hypothesis: replacement_of_unstable_or_impure_reagent, optimization_of_catalyst_loading, process_modeling_or_digital_twin_guided_change - by selecting a more robust catalyst, limiting exposure to high temperatures/pressures, or implementing regeneration steps, catalyst life is extended.
Experiment: A regeneration protocol (oxidative burn-off at 350 °C) was applied to spent Pd/C after four cycles; activity was restored to > 95 % of the fresh catalyst. Parallel runs with a more stable Pd/alumina catalyst showed no activity loss over ten cycles, allowing a 30 % reduction in catalyst inventory.
additional_details: Deactivation is accelerated when the reaction mixture contains acidic or basic impurities, high H₂ pressures, or when the substrate is prone to polymerisation. Monitoring metal content in the product stream can provide early warning.

Observation: Requirement of high H₂ pressure (>= 5 bar) together with pyrophoric or explosive reagents; reports of "pressure-related safety risk" or need for special pressure-relief devices.
Hypothesis: condition_change_to_reduce_or_remove_process_hazard, pressure_or_gas_headspace_optimization, thermal_runaway_mitigation_or_quench_safety_modification - by lowering the operating pressure (using more active catalysts or transfer-hydrogenation), adding pressure-relief valves, and implementing controlled venting sequences, the hazard is mitigated.
Experiment: The Ir-catalysed hydrogenation originally run at 5 barg was re-optimised with a more active Rh-BenzP* system, allowing operation at 1 atm H₂. A pressure-relief valve and automated vent-purge cycle were installed; no pressure excursions were observed in 100 h of continuous operation.
additional_details: Safety concerns are amplified for reactions that generate gases (Mg addition, diimide formation) or when the catalyst becomes pyrophoric after H₂ uptake. Continuous monitoring of pressure and temperature with interlocks is recommended.

Observation: Significant batch-to-batch fluctuations in conversion or selectivity (± 10 % or more) without any intentional change in recipe.
Hypothesis: process_modeling_or_digital_twin_guided_change, improved_in_process_control_or_analytical_method, custom_or_novel_reactor_design - by implementing real-time analytics (online GC, IR), building a kinetic model to predict performance, and standardising reactor hardware, variability can be reduced.
Experiment: An online GC-FID was installed on a 15 L hydrogenation loop; data were fed into a digital twin that adjusted H₂ flow to maintain a constant dissolved H₂ concentration. Over 30 runs the conversion CV dropped from ± 12 % to ± 3 %.
additional_details: Variability is especially evident for membrane-based Pd/C cartridges, for reactions with solid substrates, or when the substrate concentration approaches solubility limits. Routine catalyst activity checks and feedstock QC are also effective.

Observation: Reactor temperature climbs above the set-point (e.g., > 4 °C for a 0-2 °C Schotten-Baumann amide) during the feed-rate increase or reagent addition.
Hypothesis:
temperature_setpoint_or_temperature_ramp_optimization, change_of_base, change_of_primary_reagent 
*Lowering the addition temperature, slowing the feed, or switching to a less-exothermic reagent/base pair reduces the heat-release rate and keeps the reactor within the safe temperature window.*
Experiment: A DoE on feed-rate, inlet temperature and cooling-jacket flow was performed on a pilot-scale reactor. The optimal condition kept the residence time at 7 min, used a 0 °C inlet slurry and a cooling-jacket set-point of 2 °C. Temperature excursions were limited to <= 1 °C and conversion remained > 90 %.
additional_details:
- The symptom is most acute when the amino-acid feed is increased (e.g., from 10 min to 5 min residence). 
- The same issue appears with highly reactive acid chlorides (e.g., 4-chlorobenzoyl chloride) where HCl evolution is rapid. 
- Monitoring the temperature in real time (inline thermocouples) is essential to catch the spike early.

Observation: A solid or slurry forms in the reactor or downstream lines (e.g., fine salt precipitate, insoluble lithium salt, or polymeric sludge) that clogs pumps, filters or heat-exchange surfaces.
Hypothesis:
solvent_change_for_solubility, change_of_primary_reagent, slurry_handling_or_particle_size_optimization, improved_mixing_or_impeller_design 
*Using a more polar co-solvent, switching to a less hygroscopic salt, or adjusting particle size/feeding strategy prevents solid formation and maintains a clear flow.*
Experiment: The lithium carboxylate was replaced by the sodium analogue (entry 17787) and the acyl chloride was pre-dissolved in 10 % acetonitrile before addition (entry 8430). In a 500 L batch the slurry disappeared, pump pressure stayed constant and overall yield improved from 78 % to 92 %.
additional_details:
- Hygroscopic salts (e.g., Li-carboxylates) are especially problematic at low temperature. 
- In continuous flow, solid fouling can be mitigated by a short residence-time heat-exchange section that keeps the mixture above the solubility limit. 
- Regular hopper tapping and a high-shear impeller (>= 4000 rpm) are effective for cohesive powders (e.g., NCA solids).

Observation: The reaction mixture becomes highly viscous or forms a gel-like mass that resists stirring; impeller speed-dependent conversion drops (e.g., 61 % conversion at 5 min residence when the slurry is not fully dispersed).
Hypothesis:
improved_mixing_or_impeller_design, solvent_change_for_solubility, solvent_system_optimization_or_cosolvent_addition 
*Increasing impeller speed, adding a low-viscosity co-solvent, or using a micellar additive reduces viscosity and restores homogeneous mixing.*
Experiment: A high-shear Rushton turbine (4000 rpm) was installed in a 200 L reactor for the NCA-peptide coupling (entry 7111). Conversion rose from 61 % to 71 % and the slurry no longer adhered to the vessel wall. In parallel, adding 2 % TPGS-750-M surfactant (entry 2010) prevented agglomeration in aqueous Schotten-Baumann runs.
additional_details:
- The symptom is often observed when solid reagents are fed as powders (e.g., NCA, lithium salts). 
- Adding a small amount of co-solvent (e.g., 5 % acetonitrile in water) can dramatically lower viscosity without affecting reactivity. 
- Real-time torque monitoring helps flag the onset of a viscous regime.

Observation: Analytical data (HPLC, GC) shows the sudden appearance of a new peak (e.g., di-acylated impurity, HCN, or dimer) that grows with time or with higher reagent concentration.
Hypothesis:
change_of_additive, change_of_base, change_of_acid, optimization_of_reagent_stoichiometry, temperature_setpoint_or_temperature_ramp_optimization 
*Limiting the amount of acylating agent, switching to a weaker base, or adding a scavenger (e.g., N-methylmorpholine to trap HCN) suppresses the impurity pathway.*
Experiment: For the acryloylation of a phenolic amine (entry 17948) the base was changed from TEA to 2,6-lutidine and the acyl chloride feed was slowed. Impurity S-17 dropped from 12 % to < 1 % and overall isolated yield increased from 68 % to 85 %.
additional_details:
- Monitoring the impurity profile in real time (inline HPLC) enables early detection before the impurity exceeds specification. 
- Some impurities (e.g., HCN) are also safety concerns; their suppression is a dual benefit. 
- The impurity trend often correlates with temperature spikes, reinforcing the need to control exotherms.

Observation: Rapid gas evolution (CO₂, HCl, NH₃) is observed as bubbling or a pressure increase in a closed reactor; pressure-sensor alarms trigger when the set-point is exceeded.
Hypothesis:
pressure_or_gas_headspace_optimization, change_of_base, change_of_addition_order_or_feed_profile, improved_quench_or_neutralization 
*Using a controlled addition profile, venting the reactor, or switching to a non-gaseous base (e.g., solid K₂CO₃) mitigates pressure buildup.*
Experiment: In the CDI-activated amide coupling (entry 21530) the addition of the amine was performed via a semi-batch feed over 30 min while maintaining a nitrogen headspace. The pressure stayed within 1 bar of the set-point and the reaction gave > 99 % conversion without venting issues.
additional_details:
- For continuous flow, back-pressure regulators (8 bar) were employed to keep the system stable while allowing gas to escape through a vent. 
- Inline pressure monitoring coupled with a feedback-controlled feed pump prevented over-pressurisation. 
- Adding a scavenger (e.g., aqueous NaHCO₃) to neutralise HCl immediately after formation reduces gas evolution.

Observation: Sudden or uncontrolled increase in reactor temperature (often > 200 °C) during the hydrolysis step.
Hypothesis:
temperature_setpoint_or_temperature_ramp_optimization, improved_heat_transfer_or_temperature_control_hardware, thermal_runaway_mitigation_or_quench_safety_modification. 
Lowering the set-point or using a staged temperature ramp reduces the instantaneous heat release; better jacket design or internal coils improves heat removal; controlled quench prevents post-reaction temperature spikes.
Experiment: A DoE on temperature-ramp profiles was performed: (i) reduce the maximum reaction temperature from 240 °C to 130 °C (11051), (ii) implement a semi-batch addition of LiOH/H₂O₂ over 4 h while maintaining 25 °C (16796), and (iii) install a high-efficiency coil-in-jacket and monitor temperature with a fast-response RTD. The optimized conditions eliminated temperature overshoot in pilot-scale runs.
additional_details: The severity of the symptom scales with the amount of strong base/oxidant and with solvent boiling points (e.g., DEG vs. propylene glycol). Early detection via inline temperature probes is essential.

Observation: Visible biphasic layers, slurry formation, or high viscosity that leads to uneven reagent distribution (e.g., "precipitated" amide, "viscous" feed).
Hypothesis:
solvent_change_for_solubility, solvent_system_optimization_or_cosolvent_addition, phase_behavior_or_biphasic_system_optimization, improved_mixing_or_impeller_design, change_of_addition_order_or_feed_profile. 
Switching to a single-phase solvent system (e.g., 85 % EtOH/H₂O, 5586), adding a co-solvent to lower viscosity (7611), or using a high-speed impeller (16795) restores homogeneous mixing.
Experiment: A solvent-screening matrix (EtOH, MeOH, PG, THF) identified 85 % EtOH/H₂O as fully miscible with the substrate and base. The optimal impeller geometry (low-shear pitched-blade) was installed in the CSTR, and the TBAOH/THF streams were fed via three synchronized pumps (16795). Scale-up runs showed no phase separation and > 95 % conversion.
additional_details: Temperature influences miscibility; the optimal range (24-25 °C) was selected to avoid THF/H₂O phase splitting (16792). Monitoring torque on the agitator can serve as an early warning.

Observation: Rapid generation of gas (O₂, H₂) that raises head-space pressure or creates bubbling, sometimes exceeding safety limits (> 2.5 % v/v O₂).
Hypothesis:
gas_evolution_or_mass_transfer_management, pressure_or_gas_headspace_optimization, change_of_additive. 
Implementing a nitrogen sweep (16789), controlling addition rate of peroxide (16793), and venting to a scrubber mitigate pressure spikes.
Experiment: A semi-batch addition of H₂O₂ over 4 h under a continuous N₂ blanket was tested in a 250 mL CSTR equipped with a pressure-relief valve. Inline O₂ sensor triggered automatic shutdown when O₂ > 2 % v/v. The modified protocol eliminated over-pressure events in kilogram-scale runs.
additional_details: Gas evolution is temperature-dependent; maintaining low reaction temperature (<= 25 °C) reduces O₂ generation rate. Proper vent sizing is critical for safety compliance.

Observation: Stagnant conversion (< 80 %) or appearance of a specific impurity (hydroxy-amide, per-acid by-product) that grows with scale.
Hypothesis:
optimization_of_acid_or_base_stoichiometry, change_of_primary_reagent, change_of_additive, optimization_of_reagent_stoichiometry. 
Increasing H₂O₂ equivalents suppresses hydroxy-amide (16798 -> 16798 solution), adjusting base concentration improves conversion (17258), and adding scavengers or buffers can limit side-reactions.
Experiment: A factorial DoE varied H₂O₂ (2-6 equiv) and LiOH (1.2-2.0 equiv) while monitoring hydroxy-amide impurity by HPLC. The optimum (4.6 equiv H₂O₂, 1.6 equiv LiOH) gave > 99 % conversion with <= 5 % impurity (16793).
additional_details: Impurity profiles are sensitive to water content; precise control of solvent water concentration (9.5 M) is required (16969). Real-time HPLC can flag impurity rise early.

Observation: Formation of fine solids or slurries that block filters, pumps, or cause reactor fouling (17256, 17260, 7615).
Hypothesis:
clogging_or_fouling_mitigation, slurry_handling_or_particle_size_optimization, improved_mixing_or_impeller_design, phase_behavior_or_biphasic_system_optimization. 
Diluting the mixture before filtration, adding a co-solvent (MeOH) to keep solids suspended, and installing inline filters prevent blockage.
Experiment: A scale-up trial added 20 % v/v MeOH to the hydrolysate before filtration and employed a 10 µm mesh filter downstream of the reactor. Filtration time dropped from > 2 h to < 30 min, and no fouling was observed over multiple batches (17256).
additional_details: Temperature control during antisolvent addition (maintain 45-50 °C) reduces sudden nucleation (20900). Monitoring slurry particle size with laser diffraction can guide solvent addition rates.

Observation: Sudden, uncontrolled rise in reactor temperature (hot-spot) during bromine or NBS addition.
Hypothesis: temperature_setpoint_or_temperature_ramp_optimization, change_of_addition_order_or_feed_profile, improved_heat_transfer_or_temperature_control_hardware - controlling the addition rate, lowering the set-point, and improving heat removal will keep the temperature rise within the design envelope and prevent hot-spots.
Experiment:
- Conduct calorimetric studies to quantify the heat-release profile. 
- Implement semi-batch feeding of bromine/NBS (e.g. 5-10 min aliquots) while actively cooling with a jacket capable of >= 2 kW removal. 
- Verify temperature stability with in-line thermocouples; repeat at pilot-scale (~ 100 kg) to confirm no temperature excursions > 5 °C.
additional_details: Hot-spot severity correlates with reagent concentration and reactor geometry; lower reagent concentration or use of a co-solvent can further dampen the exotherm. For photochemical brominations, LED-generated heat must also be managed by water-cooled panels.

Observation: Formation of slurries, solid NBS suspensions, or emulsions that give uneven mixing, localized over-bromination, or poor mass-transfer.
Hypothesis: improved_mixing_or_impeller_design, solvent_change_for_solubility, solvent_system_optimization_or_cosolvent_addition - redesign impeller geometry, increase agitation speed, or switch to a solvent that fully dissolves solid reagents to obtain a homogeneous reaction mixture.
Experiment:
- Test NBS solutions (e.g. 6 wt % in MeCN) versus solid addition in a 4 L reactor equipped with a downward-impeller stirrer at >= 800 rpm. 
- Evaluate slurry-feed pumps for continuous dosing of bromine/NBS. 
- Perform DoE on solvent/cosolvent ratios (MeCN/EtOAc, MeCN/DMSO) to achieve complete dissolution at the target concentration (~ 0.2 M). 
- Scale to kilogram batch and monitor conversion uniformity by in-process sampling.
additional_details: Mixing problems are amplified when the reaction is highly exothermic; thus, the mixing solution should be paired with temperature control. For biphasic systems (e.g., aqueous HBr/organic substrate) a slug-flow or high-shear pump may be required.

Observation: Batch-to-batch fluctuations in conversion or impurity levels when using reagents from different suppliers or with differing impurity profiles (e.g., NBS containing variable Br₂/HBr).
Hypothesis: feedstock_or_supplier_variability_management, optimization_of_reagent_stoichiometry, change_of_additive - qualify suppliers, set tighter impurity specifications, and adjust stoichiometry or add chelating additives to buffer the effect of impurities.
Experiment:
- Perform a small-scale qualification test for each new NBS lot (e.g., 5 g reaction, monitor conversion). 
- Use kinetic modeling to define a conservative NBS equivalence (e.g., 1.40 eq) that ensures > 98 % conversion for both high- and low-Br₂ batches. 
- Add 5 mol % citric-acid (or NTA/EDTA) to chelate trace Cu that slows photobromination. 
- Document acceptance criteria and implement a lot-release protocol.
additional_details: When a critical impurity (e.g., Cu) is identified, the additive strategy can be more cost-effective than re-qualifying the supplier. For very reactive reagents (Br₂), consider generating bromine in-situ to standardize concentration.

Observation: Rapid generation of gaseous HBr or Br₂ leading to increased reactor head-space pressure, venting issues, or bubbling that disturbs flow rates.
Hypothesis: pressure_or_gas_headspace_optimization, improved_quench_or_neutralization, change_of_addition_order_or_feed_profile - design reactors with appropriate venting, use gas-scrubbing (NaOH, Na₂S₂O₃), and add reagents in a way that limits instantaneous gas formation.
Experiment:
- Install a PTFE-lined CSTR with a vented head-space and a downstream NaOH scrubber for HBr. 
- Switch to a semi-batch addition where the organic substrate is added slowly to a pre-cooled Br₂/HBr mixture, keeping the temperature < 35 °C (as in entry 21151). 
- Measure pressure transients with a pressure transducer; adjust feed rates until pressure rise stays below design limit (e.g., 0.5 bar).
additional_details: For photochemical brominations, the gas-generation step may be coupled with the light source; ensure that the reactor material is compatible with HBr (e.g., PTFE, glass). In batch reactors, use a nitrogen blanket to displace evolved gases safely.

Observation: Persistent oil-in-water emulsions during work-up or quench, causing phase-separation failures and product loss.
Hypothesis: solvent_change_for_solubility, phase_behavior_or_biphasic_system_optimization, improved_quench_or_neutralization - change the work-up solvent system to break emulsions, adjust pH, or add salts/anti-emulsifiers to promote clear phase separation.
Experiment:
- Replace the aqueous work-up with a MeCN-water mixture (4:1) that precipitates the product and collapses the emulsion (as in entry 7415). 
- Add a brine wash or a small amount of sodium chloride to increase ionic strength and break the emulsion. 
- Test alternative quench agents (NaOH instead of KOH) that give cleaner phase splits (entry 21194). 
- Verify recovery by measuring product concentration in both phases after separation.
additional_details: The choice of quench (e.g., Na₂S₂O₃ for bromine) can also affect emulsion stability; a dilute quench at low temperature often minimizes emulsion formation. For large-scale reactors, a continuous centrifuge can be employed if emulsions persist.

Observation: Reaction mixture becomes a thick slurry or highly viscous suspension (often after addition of solid base or formation of inorganic salts).
Hypothesis: solvent_change_for_solubility, solvent_system_optimization_or_cosolvent_addition, improved_mixing_or_impeller_design, change_of_base - switching to a liquid, soluble base (e.g., DBU) or adding a co-solvent reduces slurry formation; redesigning agitation or increasing solvent volume restores homogeneous mixing.
Experiment: A DoE was run varying (i) base (NaOtBu -> DBU), (ii) solvent composition (toluene -> toluene/MeCN 1:1), and (iii) impeller speed (400 -> 800 rpm). Conversions were measured at 1 kg scale; the optimal combination (DBU, 1:1 MeCN/toluene, 800 rpm) gave >95 % conversion with a clear solution.
additional_details: Viscosity problems are especially acute in flow (tubular reactors) where solid precipitation can cause clogging. Even in batch, high-loading solid bases can generate "slurry" that settles, leading to hot spots. Choice of base and solvent must also respect substrate stability.

Symptom: Pressure spikes / clogging in continuous flow
Observation: Sudden pressure excursions, back-pressure regulator trips, or tube blockage when the reaction is run in flow.
Hypothesis: pressure_or_gas_headspace_optimization, clogging_or_fouling_mitigation, phase_behavior_or_biphasic_system_optimization, improved_mixing_or_impeller_design - enlarge tubing or add a vented back-pressure regulator, use ultrasonic agitation, or switch to a biphasic solvent system that keeps salts dissolved in the aqueous phase.
Experiment: A pilot-scale flow of the Cu-catalysed amination (aryl bromide + amine) was run in 3 mm ID tubing with a vented BPR (1 bar). Parallel runs compared (a) original 10 mm ID tubing, (b) 7.94 mm ID tubing, and (c) 7.94 mm ID plus an inline ultrasonic bath. Only the ultrasonic-assisted run avoided blockage; pressure remained <=0.8 bar throughout 10 h operation.
additional_details: Clogging is often aggravated by temperature ramps that precipitate salts; maintaining a constant temperature and using a solvent/antisolvent pair that solubilises inorganic by-products is a robust mitigation.

Observation: Rapid temperature rise (ΔT > 30 °C) or hot spots observed during exothermic coupling, sometimes leading to uncontrolled reaction or decomposition.
Hypothesis: temperature_setpoint_or_temperature_ramp_optimization, thermal_runaway_mitigation_or_quench_safety_modification, improved_heat_transfer_or_temperature_control_hardware - implement controlled temperature ramps, external cooling jackets, or staged addition of reagents to spread the heat release.
Experiment: A calorimetric study quantified the heat of reaction (-135 kJ mol⁻¹). The batch reactor was equipped with a jacket capable of 5 kW cooling. A ramp from 0 °C to 25 °C over 2 h was programmed before holding at 50 °C. Temperature spikes were eliminated, and product purity improved from 92 % to >98 % with no Pd black formation.
additional_details: In flow, the same principle is achieved by reducing residence time or increasing the reactor surface-to-volume ratio (larger diameter tubing). Monitoring with inline IR thermography helps detect early hot spots.

Observation: Small changes in dissolved oxygen cause inconsistent conversion or longer reaction times; batches show "low conversion" when oxygen is not rigorously excluded.
Hypothesis: optimization_of_oxygen_or_gas_enriched_environment, improved_in_process_control_or_analytical_method, change_of_additive - purge reactors with inert gas, use sealed vessels, and monitor O₂ with inline sensors; optionally add oxygen-scavenging additives (e.g., phosphine-oxide scavengers).
Experiment: A scale-up (200 kg) was performed in a 500 L stainless reactor. Prior to charge, the vessel was sparged three times with nitrogen and then sealed. An inline dissolved-oxygen probe was installed; O₂ was kept <5 ppm. Conversion improved from 70 % (no purge) to >95 % with the purge protocol.
additional_details: Even trace water can exacerbate oxygen effects; drying solvents and reagents together with O₂ control gives the most robust outcome.

Observation: Reactions require >= 24 h (batch) or > 30 min residence (flow) to reach acceptable conversion, limiting throughput.
Hypothesis: hold_time_or_residence_time_optimization, optimization_of_catalyst_loading, change_of_catalyst_or_ligand_identity, optimization_of_reagent_stoichiometry - increase catalyst/ligand loading, switch to a more active Pd-ligand system, raise temperature, or use a more reactive electrophile (e.g., bromide -> iodide) to accelerate the reaction.
Experiment: A DoE varying catalyst loading (0.2 -> 0.8 mol %), temperature (80 -> 110 °C), and ligand (Xantphos -> tBuXPhos) was performed on the copper-catalysed amination of 6-bromoquinoline. The optimal condition (0.5 mol % Cu, 110 °C, tBuXPhos) reduced reaction time from 48 h to 6 h while maintaining >92 % isolated yield.
additional_details: When temperature is increased, side-product formation must be monitored; a balance between rate acceleration and impurity control is essential.

Observation:
A thick, heterogeneous slurry or solid precipitate appears during the
reaction (often at reflux or high temperature).
Hypothesis:
solvent_change_for_solubility, improved_mixing_or_impeller_design,
phase_behavior_or_biphasic_system_optimization,
slurry_handling_or_particle_size_optimization - switching to a
solvent or biphasic system that dissolves the base, or reducing particle
size, restores a single-phase mixture and improves mixing and heat
removal.
Experiment:
Screen a small DoE of solvents (e.g., THF/H₂O, toluene/water, MeCN/H₂O)
and base particle size (200 mesh vs. 325 mesh). Select the combination
that gives a clear homogeneous reaction at the target temperature, then
run a pilot-scale batch with a high-speed impeller (>=300 rpm) and monitor
temperature uniformity and conversion.
additional_details:
Viscosity spikes are especially problematic in refluxing isopropyl-acetate
or high-boiling solvents; a biphasic system also enables easy phase-transfer
catalysis. If slurry persists, consider a pre-dissolved aqueous base
(phase-behavior optimization) before scaling further.

Observation:
Final assay shows < 90 % conversion or significant residual starting
material after the prescribed reaction time.
Hypothesis:
optimization_of_reagent_stoichiometry, solvent_change_for_solubility,
change_of_base, optimization_of_acid_or_base_stoichiometry - adjusting
equivalents, selecting a solvent that fully dissolves all components, or
switching to a more soluble inorganic base (e.g., Na₂CO₃, K₃PO₄) restores
complete conversion.
Experiment:
Perform a factorial DoE varying (i) base identity (K₂CO₃, Na₂CO₃, K₃PO₄),
(ii) solvent (acetone, MeCN, DMF, THF/H₂O), and (iii) electrophile
equivalents (1.0-1.3 eq). Measure conversion at the target time; adopt the
optimal set for a kilogram-scale run and verify that residual starting
material falls below 2 %.
additional_details:
When the electrophile is a liquid bromide with limited solubility (e.g.,
t-butyl-2-bromoacetate), co-solvent addition (toluene/H₂O) can dramatically
improve dissolution. Beware of side-reactions introduced by stronger bases;
monitor impurity profiles concurrently.

Symptom: Impurity surge at high temperature / concentration
Observation:
A specific impurity (e.g., enantiomer, allene, dimer) exceeds its specification
once temperature or reagent concentration is increased.
Hypothesis:
improved_impurity_purge_or_byproduct_control,
temperature_setpoint_or_temperature_ramp_optimization,
change_of_base, change_of_additive - lowering the temperature setpoint,
optimising the ramp, or switching to a base/additive that suppresses the
side pathway can keep impurity levels below limits.
Experiment:
Run a temperature-profile study (30 °C -> 70 °C) while holding reagent
equivalents constant. Identify the temperature where impurity formation
begins (e.g., > 0.25 % enantiomer). Implement a controlled ramp or
operate at the lower temperature with a slight excess of electrophile to
maintain conversion. Validate on a pilot-scale batch with in-process HPLC.
additional_details:
Impurities often arise from base-promoted elimination (allene) or
phase-transfer-catalyst-mediated over-alkylation. Adding a catalytic
acid (e.g., AcOH 0.25 eq) can suppress dimer formation (see entry 3215).
Monitoring temperature gradients in the reactor is critical to avoid local
hot spots.

Symptom: Excess reagent waste / high material cost
Observation:
Large excesses of expensive reagents (e.g., bromides, bases, solvents) are
used to achieve target conversion, leading to high raw-material cost and
large waste streams.
Hypothesis:
optimization_of_reagent_stoichiometry,
replacement_of_costly_or_low_purity_reagent,
replacement_of_unstable_or_impure_reagent - tightening equivalents,
substituting cheaper bromides or bases, or using in-situ generated reagents
reduces cost and waste without sacrificing yield.
Experiment:
Conduct a virtual DoE (or actual DoE) varying bromide equivalents from
1.0 to 1.5 eq and base equivalents from 1.0 to 2.0 eq. Track conversion,
impurity profile, and material cost. Select the minimal excess that still
delivers > 98 % conversion. Where possible, replace expensive bases (e.g.,
Cs₂CO₃) with K₂CO₃ or Na₂CO₃, and replace costly PTCs with catalytic
TBAB.
additional_details:
Cost optimisation must be balanced against impurity control; a slight
excess may be justified if it suppresses a problematic side-product.
Re-evaluate downstream work-up to ensure that reduced excess does not
increase isolation difficulty.

Observation:
Rapid temperature rise (> 10 °C above setpoint) or uncontrolled exotherm
during reagent addition or reaction progress.
Hypothesis:
temperature_setpoint_or_temperature_ramp_optimization,
thermal_runaway_mitigation_or_quench_safety_modification,
improved_heat_transfer_or_temperature_control_hardware,
change_of_addition_order_or_feed_profile - controlling addition rate,
using jacketed reactors with efficient heat removal, and implementing
quench-safety steps mitigate the exotherm.
Experiment:
Design a semi-batch addition study: feed the bromide substrate over 30 min
while monitoring reactor temperature with an inline probe. Compare
continuous addition, split-charge, and slow-drip addition. Install a
jacketed reactor with a high-capacity coolant and validate that the
temperature never exceeds the safety limit (e.g., 45 °C). Scale the optimized
addition profile to kilogram scale and confirm reproducible temperature
control.
additional_details:
When CO is used (carbonylation) pressure-related exotherms may also arise;
venting or pressure-control loops are required (see entry 15639). Adding
an external quench (e.g., aqueous Na₂S₂O₃ for CNBr) can also neutralise
heat-generating species.

Observation: A solid base or reagent (e.g., K₂CO₃, CuI, Bpin ester) forms a thick slurry or suspension that is difficult to stir uniformly in batch reactors.
Hypothesis: improved_mixing_or_impeller_design, solvent_system_optimization_or_cosolvent_addition, batch_to_flow_or_flow_process_implementation - better agitation, a co-solvent to keep all components in solution, or a flow reactor with static mixers will eliminate the slurry, improve contact and give reproducible conversion.
Experiment: A DoE screening of impeller type (Rushton vs. pitched-blade) and agitation speed was performed on a 10 L reactor; simultaneously, a 10 % v/v THF co-solvent was added to the DMA/K₂CO₃ system. Parallel runs in a continuous-flow tube with a static-mixing element were also evaluated. The optimal condition (high-speed pitched-blade + 10 % THF) gave quantitative conversion and uniform temperature profiles.
additional_details: The slurry issue is more pronounced with high-loading inorganic bases; milling the base (as in entry 3942) helps but does not fully solve mass-transfer limits. Switching to a homogeneous base (e.g., Cs₂CO₃) can also be considered if compatible with the substrate.

Observation: The reaction mixture separates into two immiscible liquid layers (e.g., aqueous/organic) immediately after reagent addition, giving a limited interfacial area and sluggish conversion.
Hypothesis: solvent_change_for_solubility, solvent_system_optimization_or_cosolvent_addition, phase_behavior_or_biphasic_system_optimization - selecting a single-phase solvent system or adding a miscible co-solvent (e.g., DMA, MeCN) will keep all reagents in one phase and restore mass-transfer efficiency.
Experiment: A solvent-screening matrix (DMA, MeCN, DMSO, 1,4-dioxane) was performed at 0.5 M substrate concentration. The best performance was achieved with DMA/MeCN (7:3 v/v), which dissolved both the aryl bromide and the aqueous base, eliminating the biphasic barrier and raising isolated yield from 45 % to 82 % on a 20 g scale.
additional_details: When the reaction must remain biphasic (e.g., for downstream work-up), vigorous stirring and the use of phase-transfer catalysts (e.g., tetrabutylammonium bromide) can mitigate the issue, but a single-phase system is preferred for robustness.

Observation: During the addition of a reagent (hydrazone, CsOH, or a solid base) the reactor temperature rises abruptly (often > 30 °C above setpoint) and can exceed the catalyst's stability window.
Hypothesis: temperature_setpoint_or_temperature_ramp_optimization, thermal_runaway_mitigation_or_quench_safety_modification, improved_heat_transfer_or_temperature_control_hardware, change_of_addition_order_or_feed_profile - controlling the addition rate (syringe pump), pre-cooling the feed, and using a jacketed reactor with efficient cooling will damp the exotherm.
Experiment: A controlled-feed study was carried out: the hydrazone was delivered over 3 h via a syringe pump into a jacketed 25 L reactor held at 25 °C. An external cooling loop maintained the bulk temperature within ±2 °C. The temperature spike was eliminated, conversion rose to 94 % and no catalyst decomposition was observed.
additional_details: Even with controlled addition, the presence of gas-evolving bases (Na₂CO₃) can cause pressure rise; coupling the temperature control with venting (pressure-or-gas-headspace optimization) is advisable for very large batches.

Observation: Identical reaction set-ups give widely different conversions (e.g., 50 %-90 %) when the scale is increased from milligram to gram levels.
Hypothesis: optimization_of_catalyst_loading, change_of_catalyst_or_ligand_identity, change_of_primary_reagent, optimization_of_reagent_stoichiometry - fixing a robust catalyst/ligand pair (e.g., ethylene-Rh precursor, t-Bu₂MeP) and defining a narrow loading window removes the source of variability.
Experiment: A catalyst-loading DoE (0.25 mol % -> 0.75 mol %) was performed on a 5 g scale using the Rh-Segphos system. The ethylene-Rh precursor gave consistent conversion (~80 %) across the loading range, whereas the original RhCl₂ dimer showed > 30 % spread. The optimized loading (0.5 mol %) was adopted for all subsequent scales.
additional_details: Supplier-to-supplier variability of the aryl bromide (impurities, moisture) can also cause conversion spread; implementing a feedstock variability management protocol (entry 31) further stabilizes the process.

Observation: Significant amounts of side-products (e.g., protodesilylation products, dimeric hydrazone adducts, biaryl dimers) appear, lowering isolated yield and complicating purification.
Hypothesis: change_of_base, change_of_additive, improved_impurity_purge_or_byproduct_control, solvent_change_to_reduce_side_products - milder bases (NaOt-Bu vs. LiO-t-Bu), additives that suppress side pathways (CuI, water-containing Cs₂CO₃), or solvents that improve substrate stability (MeOH cosolvent) will curb impurity formation.
Experiment: A systematic base-screen (LiO-t-Bu, NaOt-Bu, Cs₂CO₃.2 H₂O) was conducted for the silanol coupling (entry 10876). NaOt-Bu reduced protodesilylation from 35 % to < 5 % and increased product yield from 42 % to 78 %. Parallel addition of 0.05 equiv CuI further suppressed dimer formation in the Barluenga reaction (entry 3933).
additional_details: Impurity-control strategies often need to be paired with downstream purification tweaks (e.g., aqueous work-up, crystallization solvent optimization) to achieve the required purity for API intermediates.

Observation: Stable oil-in-water emulsion that does not break on cooling; phase-boundary is fuzzy or "slurry-to-slurry" persists.
Hypothesis: solvent_change_for_solubility, solvent_system_optimization_or_cosolvent_addition, phase_behavior_or_biphasic_system_optimization, improved_mixing_or_impeller_design, change_of_additive
Experiment: Screen alternative aqueous/organic solvent systems (e.g., TPGS-750-M + acetone, TL-82 surfactant blend, THF -> toluene) and/or add a low-viscosity cosolvent; evaluate mixing hardware (high-shear homogenizer, overhead stirrer) and quantify phase-clearance time.
additional_details: The symptom often appears only after scale-up (different vessel geometry, larger volume) even when small-scale screens look clean. Early visual check of the reaction bulk after reagent addition is a cheap diagnostic.

Observation: Temperature jumps > 30 °C within 1-2 min after addition of catalyst or aqueous base; ΔT exceeds solvent boiling point in pilot runs.
Hypothesis: temperature_setpoint_or_temperature_ramp_optimization, improved_heat_transfer_or_temperature_control_hardware, change_of_addition_order_or_feed_profile, pressure_or_gas_headspace_optimization, thermal_runaway_mitigation_or_quench_safety_modification
Experiment: Perform calorimetry on a small scale to obtain ΔH and adiabatic temperature rise; then implement a staged addition (pre-cool reagents, semi-batch feed) and/or upgrade jacket/heat-exchanger capacity; monitor temperature with fast-response probes.
additional_details: A modest temperature rise is acceptable; the key is to keep the bulk temperature below the solvent's safe limit and below the decomposition onset of reagents (e.g., DMSO, THF).

Observation: Formation of solid particles (e.g., black Pd-black, polymeric BBA, inorganic salts) that deposit on walls or block flow channels; visible slurry becomes gritty.
Hypothesis: clogging_or_fouling_mitigation, solvent_change_for_solubility, solvent_change_for_safety_or_green_chemistry, phase_behavior_or_biphasic_system_optimization, improved_mixing_or_impeller_design
Experiment: Test alternative solvents/co-solvents that keep all reagents in solution (e.g., replace 1,4-dioxane with 2-MeTHF, add ethylene glycol to BBA, switch THF -> toluene for aryl chlorides); evaluate filtration or inline solids-removal devices.
additional_details: Early visual inspection after the first 5 min can reveal precipitation; a quick solubility check of each component at reaction temperature is a preventive step.

Observation: Pd measured > 50 ppm (or > 10 ppm for API) after standard work-up; metal-scavenger cartridges give < 70 % removal; chromatography required.
Hypothesis: improved_impurity_purge_or_byproduct_control, change_of_additive, drying_or_isolation_process_optimization, crystallization_solvent_or_antisolvent_optimization, step_reordering_or_telescope_strategy
Experiment: Introduce a dedicated Pd-scavenging step (e.g., N-acetyl-cysteine aqueous wash, polymer-bound scavenger, metal-chelating resin) and verify removal by ICP-OES; alternatively redesign the sequence to avoid Pd-containing intermediates (telescoping, in-line quench).
additional_details: The symptom is often discovered only after analytical testing; a quick test strip for Pd can be used on-line to trigger the scavenger step before scale-up.

Observation: Same recipe gives 40 % conversion on one batch, > 90 % on another; often linked to impurity (sulfur, oxygen) in starting material or to batch-to-batch Pd loading.
Hypothesis: change_of_additive, change_of_base, change_of_primary_reagent, optimization_of_catalyst_loading, feedstock_or_supplier_variability_management, tolerance_of_reagent_or_feed_impurities
Experiment: Perform impurity profiling of raw materials (e.g., sulfur content by elemental analysis); if impurity present, add a scavenger (N-acetyl-cysteine) or switch to a cleaner reagent (e.g., use aryl chloride instead of bromide that carries less sulfur); adjust Pd loading based on impurity level.
additional_details: Early QC of each lot of electrophile (e.g., check for elemental sulfur) can prevent downstream poisoning; a small "spike" test with extra Pd can be used as a diagnostic.

Observation: A solid layer of inorganic carbonate/bicarbonate salts accumulates at the organic/aqueous boundary, making phase separation difficult and causing material loss.
Hypothesis: solvent_change_for_solubility, optimization_of_acid_or_base_stoichiometry - switching to a solvent that reduces the inorganic salt load (e.g., 2-MeTHF) and lowering the base equivalents (NaHCO₃ 2.5 eq) will keep salts dissolved or in a fine slurry that can be removed cleanly.
Experiment: A solvent-screen DoE (TBME, 2-MeTHF, MTBE) combined with base-equivalence screening (Na₂CO₃ 1 eq, NaHCO₃ 2.5 eq, no base) was run on a 30 L pilot. The optimal condition (2-MeTHF + NaHCO₃ 2.5 eq) gave a clear phase split and restored the 85 % isolated yield.
additional_details: The symptom becomes more pronounced when the aqueous phase is highly concentrated (>0.5 M carbonate). Maintaining the aqueous pH near neutral (~8.5) also helps keep salts soluble.

Observation: Rapid temperature rise (often >30 °C within minutes) upon addition of a reagent (e.g., isocyanate, chlorosulfonyl isocyanate, BocX) - sometimes exceeding the set-point and causing overheating.
Hypothesis: temperature_setpoint_or_temperature_ramp_optimization, batch_to_flow_or_flow_process_implementation, improved_heat_transfer_or_temperature_control_hardware - controlling addition rate, using low-temperature feeds, or moving to a plug-flow reactor with high surface-to-volume ratio mitigates the exotherm.
Experiment: A semi-batch addition profile was programmed: the exothermic reagent was fed over 2 h while the reactor temperature was held at 5 °C (jacket). Parallel flow experiments used a 0.5 L PFR with a 30 s residence time and a 0 °C jacket. Both approaches kept the bulk temperature <=10 °C and eliminated product degradation.
additional_details: The severity scales with reagent concentration; dilute feeds (<=0.5 M) are preferred. For very fast exotherms (CSI, BocX) a micro-reactor is often the only safe option.

Observation: Formation of a thick, pasty slurry or solid deposits that cling to the reactor wall, accompanied by uneven stirring and localized "hot-spots".
Hypothesis: change_of_additive, improved_mixing_or_impeller_design, phase_behavior_or_biphasic_system_optimization - adding a static mixer, using a peristaltic pump with a viscous-solvent kit, or pre-heating the viscous feed to lower viscosity resolves the mixing limitation.
Experiment: A Kenics static mixer was installed in the feed line of the HDIT/MEKO reaction; the HDIT feed was pre-heated to 75 °C to drop viscosity below 500 mPa.s. The slurry remained fluid, temperature remained uniform, and conversion reached >95 % with no pressure drop.
additional_details: The symptom is aggravated when the product viscosity exceeds 10 000 mPa.s. Short residence-time reactors (PFR) are preferred for such highly viscous streams.

Observation: Visible gas evolution (bubbling, pressure increase) when a chloro-formate or isocyanate is added; occasional detection of HCl or CO₂ in the vent stream.
Hypothesis: change_of_primary_reagent, condition_change_to_reduce_or_remove_process_hazard, improved_quench_or_neutralization - replacing the hazardous gas-generating reagent with a safer alternative (e.g., potassium cyanate instead of tert-butyl isocyanate) or adding an acid scavenger (pyridine, lutidine) and venting through a scrubber eliminates the hazard.
Experiment: A comparative run substituted Cbz-Cl with Fmoc-Cl (lower HCl release) and introduced pyridine (2 eq) as an HCl scavenger. Gas-flow meters showed a >90 % reduction in HCl evolution, and the reaction proceeded with identical conversion.
additional_details: When the gas is unavoidable (e.g., Boc-protection), the addition must be temperature-controlled (<=30 °C) and vent lines equipped with alkaline scrubbers.

Observation: When the aqueous pH is above the target (e.g., pH 11 instead of pH 9), a significant amount (~5-10 %) of a symmetrical over-acylated urea or bis-acyl impurity appears.
Hypothesis: optimization_of_acid_or_base_stoichiometry, optimization_of_acid_or_base_stoichiometry - tightening the buffer system (phosphate buffer at pH 9) and limiting base equivalents (NaHCO₃ 2.5 eq) keeps the reaction in the optimal pH window, suppressing over-acylation.
Experiment: A DoE varying K₂HPO₄ concentration and KOH addition was performed on a 20 L batch. The optimal condition (pH 9 ± 0.2) reduced impurity 34 from 9 % to <0.2 % while maintaining >99 % conversion.
additional_details: The symptom is more acute for highly nucleophilic amines and when the electrophile is a highly reactive chloroformate. Real-time pH monitoring with an inline probe is recommended for large scale.

Observation: The reaction mixture becomes a thick, highly viscous slurry that is difficult to stir or pump.
Hypothesis: improved_mixing_or_impeller_design, solvent_change_for_solubility, solvent_system_optimization_or_cosolvent_addition - upgrading impeller speed or geometry and/or switching to a higher-solubility solvent/co-solvent reduces viscosity and restores homogeneous mixing.
Experiment: Conduct a DoE varying impeller speed (100 -> 1200 rpm) and solvent composition (e.g., adding 10 % v/v DMSO or NMP to the original aqueous/organic system). Measure slurry viscosity, conversion, and filtration time at pilot scale. Select the combination that yields a low-viscosity, fully mixed slurry with >= 95 % conversion.
additional_details: Viscosity often rises when the amine is present as a salt or when the reaction is run at high substrate concentration. Adding a small amount of a polar aprotic co-solvent (DMSO, NMP) or a low-boiling organic solvent (2-MeTHF) can dramatically lower the slurry's resistance to stirring without compromising downstream work-up.

Observation: A rapid, uncontrolled rise in reaction temperature (10-20 °C) occurs when a base or nucleophile is added (e.g., during amine addition).
Hypothesis: temperature_setpoint_or_temperature_ramp_optimization, improved_heat_transfer_or_temperature_control_hardware - applying a controlled, slower addition profile and/or upgrading the jacket/heat-exchange hardware keeps the temperature within the safe window.
Experiment: Implement a semi-batch feed where the amine solution is added over 30 min while monitoring temperature with an inline probe. Compare a standard addition (instant) versus a ramped addition (0 -> 30 min) and evaluate conversion, impurity profile, and temperature excursions. If needed, install a higher-capacity heat-exchanger and repeat the test.
additional_details: The magnitude of the spike correlates with the stoichiometric excess of the base and the heat capacity of the solvent. Using a lower-boiling, higher-heat-capacity solvent (e.g., MeCN) or diluting the base in a larger volume can also dampen the temperature rise.

Observation: A new impurity (e.g., over-alkylated amide, dimer, or N-acylurea) appears at >= 0.5 % and grows rapidly as the scale increases.
Hypothesis: optimization_of_reagent_stoichiometry, change_of_additive, change_of_base - tightening the equivalents of amine/reagent, adjusting the addition sequence, or switching to a less nucleophilic base suppresses the competing pathway.
Experiment: Run a series of small-scale trials varying (i) amine equivalents (0.9 -> 1.2 eq), (ii) base identity (triethylamine, DIPEA, potassium carbonate), and (iii) addition order (base -> acid -> amine vs. simultaneous). Analyze impurity levels by LC-MS. Scale the optimal condition to pilot batch and confirm impurity suppression.
additional_details: Impurities often arise from carbodiimide activation (e.g., formation of N-acylurea) or from excess amine driving over-alkylation. Using a staged addition of the amine or employing a less nucleophilic inorganic base can dramatically reduce these by-products.

Symptom: Clogging or flow instability in continuous reactors
Observation: During continuous-flow operation the reactor experiences pressure spikes, pump trips, or solid bridging, leading to flow interruption.
Hypothesis: clogging_or_fouling_mitigation, custom_or_novel_reactor_design, improved_mixing_or_impeller_design - redesigning the mixer (e.g., V-shaped micro-mixer), increasing tubing diameter, or adding inline filtration mitigates blockage.
Experiment: Compare three reactor configurations: (i) standard PFA tubing (1 mm ID), (ii) larger-ID tubing (2 mm), and (iii) a custom V-shaped static mixer. Run the same reaction at identical residence time while monitoring pressure, flow rate, and product quality. Select the configuration that eliminates pressure excursions and maintains conversion.
additional_details: Clogging is especially prevalent with reactions that generate insoluble salts (e.g., acid-base neutralizations) or when the product precipitates during the reaction. Adding a co-solvent to keep the product in solution or installing a periodic solvent-flush cycle can also prevent fouling.

Observation: After reaction completion the mixture forms a fine solid or slurry that is difficult to filter; filtration rates drop below 10 L min⁻¹, and wet cake weight is excessive.
Hypothesis: improved_quench_or_neutralization, solvent_change_for_solubility, drying_or_isolation_process_optimization - adjusting the quench to keep the product in solution, switching to a solvent that gives a filter-friendly precipitate, or employing a controlled crystallisation/filtration protocol resolves the bottleneck.
Experiment: Screen a set of antisolvents (e.g., IPA, EtOAc, MeCN) and temperatures (0 -> 25 °C) to identify conditions that produce a free-flowing crystalline solid. Perform a small-scale filtration test to measure cake permeability and moisture content. Implement the optimal quench/solvent system at pilot scale and compare filtration time and product recovery.
additional_details: Often the issue stems from residual water after acidification (as in entry 4116) or from a product that is only sparingly soluble in the reaction solvent. Adding a co-solvent or performing a solvent swap before work-up can dramatically improve filterability.

Observation: Sudden, uncontrolled rise in reactor temperature (often >30 °C within minutes) during reagent addition or quench.
Hypothesis: temperature_setpoint_or_temperature_ramp_optimization, improved_heat_transfer_or_temperature_control_hardware, custom_or_novel_reactor_design - lower the addition temperature, improve jacket/coil heat removal, or move to a flow reactor that dissipates heat continuously.
Experiment: Performed a DoE on addition temperature, addition rate, and jacket coolant flow. Implemented a syringe-pump addition of POCl₃ (or SO₂Cl₂) over 15 min while maintaining the reactor at -20 °C (or <=40 °C for POCl₃). In parallel, installed a high-efficiency jacket with internal coils (for batch) and a 0.030 in. PFA coil with 75 psi back-pressure (for flow). Monitored adiabatic temperature rise with calorimetry; the maximum ΔT dropped from >100 °C to <5 °C.
additional_details: The symptom is more pronounced when reagents are added in a single charge; staged or split-charge addition is often sufficient. For POCl₃-based reactions, a controlled quench with buffered aqueous solution (K₂HPO₄/K₂CO₃) further limits exotherm.

Observation: Rapid generation of gaseous HCl, SO₂, or Cl₂ leads to a rise in reactor head-space pressure; bubbling or venting is observed, sometimes causing vent-line over-pressure alarms.
Hypothesis: pressure_or_gas_headspace_optimization, gas_evolution_or_mass_transfer_management - use back-pressure regulators, gas-scrubbing loops, or design reactors that keep the gas dissolved (e.g., high-pressure flow coils).
Experiment: Installed a 8 bar back-pressure regulator on the EtOAc flow coil (α-thioamide/NCS cascade) and a sealed Hastelloy autoclave for POCl₃-mediated chlorinations. Added a drying/scrubbing bottle (conc. H₂SO₄) upstream of the reactor for Cl₂ feeds. Measured pressure profiles before and after; pressure excursions were eliminated and gas-liquid mass transfer improved, giving >85 % conversion.
additional_details: When using solid chlorinating agents (NCS, DCDMH) the gas-evolution issue is mitigated; however, for gas-phase chlorinations (Cl₂) a dedicated surge-volume and check-valve are essential to avoid back-flow.

Observation: Formation of heterogeneous suspensions or viscous slurries that are difficult to stir, cause pump blockages, or lead to uneven temperature distribution.
Hypothesis: solvent_change_for_solubility, solvent_system_optimization_or_cosolvent_addition, improved_mixing_or_impeller_design - switch to a higher-solubility solvent (e.g., sulfolane, MeCN, DMF) or add a co-solvent; redesign impeller or use high-shear mixing to keep solids in suspension.
Experiment: Screened solvents for pyrimidinone 3 (entries 4964/4966/4967) and identified sulfolane as fully dissolving both substrate and product. Implemented a 2 : 1 (v/v) 2-MeTHF/DME co-solvent system for the TMSCl-mediated chlorination (entry 7633) to achieve a stable biphasic mixture with Dₘ ~ 260. In flow, added a high-shear impeller to a 5 L stirred tank; slurry clearance time dropped from >30 min to <5 min, and residence-time distribution became uniform.
additional_details: When solubility cannot be fully achieved, limiting concentration (<=0.4 M) and using a downstream precipitation step can prevent solid buildup. For solid-forming intermediates, a rapid quench into water can lock the product out of solution.

Observation: Rapid loss of the desired chlorinated intermediate (e.g., benzylic chloride 2, chloro-oxime 7) back to the starting material or to degradation products when held at elevated temperature or exposed to moisture.
Hypothesis: optimization_of_quench_or_neutralization, change_of_primary_reagent, optimization_of_reagent_stoichiometry - quench immediately at low temperature with buffered aqueous media; replace highly unstable reagents (e.g., SOCl₂) with milder alternatives (POCl₃); adjust stoichiometry to avoid excess that drives decomposition.
Experiment: For the benzylic chloride 2 (entries 10504/10503) performed precipitation at 0 °C with water as antisolvent and reduced the reaction temperature to 0 °C during work-up, preventing hydrolysis. Replaced SOCl₂ with POCl₃ for the quinazoline chlorination (entries 21347/21350) and limited POCl₃ to 2 equiv, which eliminated the need for >20 equiv and reduced impurity formation. Conducted a time-course study showing >90 % stability of the chloro-oxime when kept at <=20 °C in DMF.
additional_details: Immediate telescoping of the unstable intermediate into the next step (e.g., coupling) is often the most robust solution. Buffer pH control (4-5) during quench avoids acid-catalyzed degradation.

Symptom: Variable conversion due to addition order / feed profile
Observation: Irreproducible assay yields and induction periods when a solid chlorinating agent (e.g., NCS, DCDMH) is added in a single charge; conversion depends on temperature or mixing speed.
Hypothesis: change_of_addition_order_or_feed_profile, optimization_of_reagent_stoichiometry - add the solid in multiple, temperature-controlled portions; use a fed-batch or continuous-flow feed to maintain a steady concentration; adjust stoichiometry to the minimum required for full conversion.
Experiment: Implemented a split-charge addition for NCS in the α-thioamide flow cascade (entries 15573/15574/15575). Compared single-charge (<=30 % conversion) vs. three-portion addition (>=85 % conversion). For DCDMH chlorinations (entries 1374/1375) introduced a three-portion, -5 °C addition, which reduced the des-TMS impurity from 5 % to <=0.2 %. Conducted a DoE varying feed ratio and temperature, confirming optimal NCS equivalents of 2.05-2.1 equiv.
additional_details: Temperature control during each addition is critical; a pre-heated substrate solution (55-60 °C) can eliminate induction periods for poorly soluble reagents like NCS in DMF.

Observation: Sudden temperature rise (>= 5-10 °C) when the basic saponification mixture is quenched with aqueous acid.
Hypothesis: temperature_setpoint_or_temperature_ramp_optimization - slow acid addition, external cooling, and temperature-controlled quench mitigate the exotherm and keep the reaction within safe limits.
Experiment: A design-of-experiments (DoE) study varied acid addition rate (dropwise vs. pump), jacket temperature, and quench temperature. The optimal condition was a controlled acid feed (<= 0.5 m L min⁻¹) into a jacket-cooled reactor (10 °C set-point), which limited the temperature spike to < 3 °C and eliminated product degradation.
additional_details: The symptom is most acute when neutralising highly concentrated NaOH/KOH solutions (>= 30 % w/w). Monitoring the temperature rise in-line (RTD) is essential for early detection.

Symptom: Poor mixability / mass-transfer limitation in biphasic systems
Observation: Incomplete conversion or dramatically prolonged reaction times when the reaction mixture is biphasic (organic / aqueous) and agitation appears insufficient.
Hypothesis: phase_behavior_or_biphasic_system_optimization, solvent_change_for_solubility, and improved_mixing_or_impeller_design - convert to a single-phase system, add a co-solvent, or redesign agitation to enhance mass transfer.
Experiment: Screened co-solvents (MeTHF, MeOH, MeCN) to achieve a homogeneous phase; the best result was 10 % v/v MeOH in THF, giving a single-phase slurry and full conversion in 2 h. Parallelly, a high-shear impeller was installed in a 200 L reactor, reducing the required residence time from 24 h to 6 h.
additional_details: The symptom often appears together with foaming (see Symptom 4) because vigorous mixing can entrain gas. Real-time phase-ratio monitoring (e.g., inline NIR) helps verify homogeneity.

Symptom: Slurry formation, high viscosity, or solid precipitation during/after hydrolysis
Observation: The reaction mixture becomes a thick, non-flowing slurry or a highly viscous suspension, leading to poor pumpability, high pressure drop, or difficulty in filtration.
Hypothesis: solvent_change_for_solubility, improved_mixing_or_impeller_design, and crystallization_solvent_or_antisolvent_optimization - select solvents that keep the reacting species in solution, dilute with a low-viscosity co-solvent, or employ antisolvent precipitation to control solid formation.
Experiment: Replaced IPA (~ 50 vol %) with isopropyl acetate (10 vol %) and added a small amount of isopropanol to lower viscosity (Symptom 2). A controlled cooling crystallisation (40 °C -> 15 °C) was introduced to precipitate the product as a filterable solid, reducing filtration pressure by 70 %.
additional_details: Viscosity issues are amplified at higher substrate concentrations; a balance between concentration (throughput) and manageable slurry rheology must be struck.

Symptom: Formation of side-products or impurities (e.g., bis-acid, N-alkylated species, racemisation)
Observation: Detectable levels of undesired impurities (>= 0.5 % LC) such as bis-acid 6', N-alkylated by-products, or racemised chiral centres appear in the crude material.
Hypothesis: improved_impurity_purge_or_byproduct_control, change_of_base, solvent_change_to_reduce_side_products, and optimization_of_reagent_stoichiometry - adjust base identity/strength, lower temperature, change solvent to drive equilibrium away from side reactions, and fine-tune equivalents.
Experiment: A DoE varying base (LiOH vs. NaOH/KOH), temperature (0 °C -> 25 °C), and solvent (MeOH, EtOH, DMF) showed that LiOH in MeOH at 0 °C suppressed bis-acid formation to < 0.1 % and eliminated N-alkylation. The optimal stoichiometry (2 equiv LiOH) was then fixed for scale-up.
additional_details: Impurity profiles should be monitored by in-process HPLC/LC-MS; early detection enables rapid adjustment of the above parameters before large batches are run.

Symptom: Temperature-sensitive decomposition or racemisation of chiral esters
Observation: Loss of stereochemical integrity (ee drops from > 96 % to < 40 %) or degradation of labile functional groups when the hydrolysis is performed above a certain temperature (often >= 30-50 °C).
Hypothesis: temperature_setpoint_or_temperature_ramp_optimization and change_of_base - operate at lower temperatures (<= 30 °C) and/or switch to a milder base (e.g., KOH in MeOH, LiOH) to preserve chiral integrity.
Experiment: A temperature-screen (10 °C -> 75 °C) with constant base loading identified 30 °C as the threshold below which racemisation of the α-chiral ester was < 1 % ee loss. The process was then transferred to a jacket-cooled flow reactor maintaining 28 °C, achieving > 99 % ee at production scale.
additional_details: When low temperature is required, reaction time may increase; this can be compensated by modestly increasing base concentration or using a more reactive solvent (e.g., MeCN) to retain throughput.

Observation: Sudden, uncontrolled rise in reactor temperature (ΔT > 30 °C) during reagent addition or when the reaction is heated.
Hypothesis: temperature_setpoint_or_temperature_ramp_optimization, change_of_addition_order_or_feed_profile, improved_heat_transfer_or_temperature_control_hardware, change_of_catalyst_or_ligand_identity - controlling the addition rate, lowering the set-point, improving heat removal, or switching to a less-exothermic catalyst can keep the temperature within a safe window.
Experiment: A Design-of-Experiments (DoE) study varying (i) addition rate of the most exothermic reagent (e.g., benzoyl chloride, thionyl chloride, dimethyl sulfate), (ii) reaction temperature set-point (0 °C -> 30 °C), and (iii) catalyst choice (Fe(OTf)₂ vs H₂SO₄). Each condition was run in a 5 L jacketed reactor equipped with a calibrated PID controller and external heat-exchange coils. Temperature profiles, conversion, and impurity levels were recorded.
additional_details:
* In cases where the exotherm is intrinsic (e.g., thionyl-chloride gas evolution), a semi-batch feed with a mass-flow controller was essential.
